name: Flesch Reading Ease
description: Scores the readability of English text from sentence length and syllables per word (Flesch 1948); higher is easier.
notes: 60–70 is plain English; below 30 is very difficult.

name: Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level
description: Converts the same counts into a US school grade (Kincaid et al. 1975); used for military manuals and insurance policies.
notes: Grade 8 is readable by most adults.

name: Gunning Fog Index

variables.label: Words of three or more syllables

description: Estimates the years of education needed to understand a text on first reading (Gunning 1952).
notes: Aim for 12 or below for a general audience.

name: SMOG Grade

variables.label: Words of three or more syllables

description: Estimates reading grade from polysyllabic words per 30 sentences (McLaughlin 1969); favoured for health information.
notes: Needs at least 30 sentences for full accuracy.

name: Coleman–Liau Index
description: Estimates reading grade from letters and sentences per 100 words, avoiding syllable counting (Coleman and Liau 1975).
notes: Easy to compute automatically.

name: Automated Readability Index
description: Estimates reading grade from characters per word and words per sentence (Smith and Senter 1967).
notes: Designed for real-time monitoring of typewriters.

name: Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve
description: Computes the share of learned material still retained after a time, using the exponential forgetting curve R = e^(−t/S).
notes: Stability S is larger for well-learned material and grows with each review; the exponential form is a simple model of Ebbinghaus's 1885 findings.

name: Hick's Law (Choice Reaction Time)
description: Computes the time to choose among n equally likely options by the Hick–Hyman law.
notes: The +1 accounts for the option of not responding. a and b are found by experiment for a task and a person.

name: Fitts's Law (Movement Time)
description: Computes the time to point at a target from its distance and width, using the Shannon form of Fitts's law.
notes: Widely used to design user interfaces: larger and closer targets are faster to hit. a and b come from measurements.

name: Fitts's Throughput
description: Computes pointing throughput, the index of difficulty divided by the movement time, as used in ISO 9241-9 to compare input devices.
notes: ISO 9241-9 uses the effective width from the spread of hits; using the nominal width gives a simpler estimate.

name: Signal Detection Sensitivity (d′)
description: Computes d′, the distance between the signal and noise distributions in standard units, from the hit and false-alarm rates.
notes: Rates of exactly 0 or 1 give an infinite result; a common fix is to replace them by 1/(2N) and 1 − 1/(2N).

name: Signal Detection Criterion (c)
description: Computes the response criterion c, which shows the bias towards saying "yes" (negative) or "no" (positive).
notes: c = 0 means no bias. It is used together with d′.

name: Deviation IQ from a Raw Score

variables.label: Standard deviation of the norm group

description: Converts a raw test score into a deviation IQ, a scale with mean 100 and standard deviation 15.
notes: The mean and standard deviation must come from the test's norm group for the same age.

name: Net Typing Speed (WPM)
description: Computes net words per minute, counting every 5 characters as one word and subtracting one word for each uncorrected error.
notes: Gross WPM leaves out the error term. Spaces and punctuation count as characters.

name: Test Score Corrected for Guessing
description: Computes the classic correction for guessing on multiple-choice tests: right answers minus wrong answers divided by (options − 1).
notes: Omitted questions are neither rewarded nor penalised. The correction assumes wrong answers come from blind guessing.

name: Reliable Change Index
description: Computes the Jacobson–Truax reliable change index, the change in a score divided by the standard error of the difference.
notes: An absolute value above 1.96 is taken as a change unlikely to be due to measurement error alone (p < 0.05).

name: Ebbinghaus Savings Score
description: Computes Ebbinghaus's savings, the percentage of the original learning effort saved when material is learned again.
notes: Savings show that memory remains even when the material cannot be recalled.

name: Kuder–Richardson 21 Reliability
description: Computes the KR-21 reliability of a test of right/wrong items from the number of items and the mean and variance of total scores.
notes: KR-21 assumes all items are equally difficult; it is never higher than KR-20.

name: Item Difficulty Index
description: Computes the difficulty index p of a test question: the proportion of students who answered it correctly.
notes: Despite the name, a higher value means an easier question. For four-option items, about 0.6–0.8 is often recommended.

name: SuperMemo SM-2 Easiness Factor Update
description: Computes the new easiness factor of a flashcard after a review in the SM-2 spaced-repetition algorithm (Woźniak, 1990).
notes: Quality 5 is a perfect answer and below 3 is a failure. The factor never falls below 1.3; the next interval is the previous one times the factor.
